summary:
Being trans is not criminalised in Ukraine. Sexual activity between men was decriminalised in 1991, sexual activity between women was never an offence, and the age of consent is 16 irrespective of gender or sexual orientation.

Legal gender recognition exists and does not require surgery. An August 2016 court ruling ordered passport and document changes for two transgender people without requiring sterilisation, and from December 2016 new identity documents are issued before any surgical procedure; married applicants and those with an underage child may also apply. The former gatekeeping was removed at the same time: applicants no longer need permission from a Ministry of Healthcare special commission, no longer petition a board of mental health professionals, and no longer spend 30 days in a psychiatric hospital, typically in wards with patients considered mentally ill.

Transsexuality nonetheless remains classified as a psychiatric disorder, and sex reassignment surgery is legal only for those over 25.

Obtaining the diagnosis that unlocks document amendment has become harder. ZMINA reported on 28 July 2026 that trans women in Ukraine now face stereotypes, corruption and wartime barriers in obtaining a diagnosis. Human Rights Watch wrote on 15 May 2024 that cross-border networks became critical support for trans women in Ukraine, arranging assessments, diagnoses and the often-humiliating confirmation by the Military Medical Commission; a Ukrainian activist described commission hours of 8am to 8pm and its gatekeeping in the words "if a doctor says I'm a woman, the state can shrug".

Border crossing is a documented friction point. Gender Stream, a Ukrainian NGO, documents that since martial law began, holders of male gender markers have been stopped at the border by the State Border Guard Service, and it helps transgender people process or reissue documents, including for those planning to cross the border legally.

Two questions were still open at the Trans Forum held in Kyiv in early June 2026: the effect of the new draft Civil Code on the transition procedure, and whether being trans grounds an exemption from mobilisation. A revised Civil Code draft submitted to Parliament on 22 January 2026 would define family as man-woman cohabitation and would automatically annul a marriage if one spouse undergoes legal sex reassignment.

Legal protection is partial. A Labor Code amendment approved by Parliament on 12 November 2015 bans gender identity discrimination at work, and in December 2022 Parliament unanimously passed a media bill banning hate speech and discrimination based on gender identity. The Criminal Code provides harsher penalties only for racial, national or religious intolerance, not gender identity: an April 2020 draft adding gender identity and sexual orientation as hate-crime grounds was withdrawn in September 2020 for lack of those terms in legislation. The rule-of-law roadmap approved by the Cabinet on 14 May 2025 plans, by Q2 2026, administrative liability for discrimination, gender identity and sexual orientation as criminal aggravating circumstances, criminal liability for public calls for violence, and free secondary legal aid.

Documented violence against LGBT people in this record is met with a weak police response. Human Rights Watch reported on 26 June 2012 that the activist Taras Karasiichuk was attacked near his Kyiv apartment, suffering a diagnosed concussion and broken jaw, in the second violent attack in six weeks after threats forced the cancellation of a pride parade; police did not immediately respond despite a medical referral, and Human Rights Watch urged an investigation into homophobic motive. Amnesty International reported on 16 May 2013 a pervasive climate of homophobia in which attacks were routinely used as a pretext to deny LGBTI people rights of expression and peaceful public events, and urged lawmakers to vote down proposals to criminalise such conduct. The most recent documented attack in this record is from June 2012; no later instance is documented.

Relationship recognition does not protect a trans visitor's marriage. Article 51 of the 1996 Constitution defines marriage as a voluntary union between a man and a woman, and Ukraine recognises no same-sex marriage or civil partnership. Courts have moved toward de facto status for same-sex couples: on 10 June 2025 the Desnianskyi District Court recognised actual marital relations between two Ukrainian men, the first such ruling in Ukraine, and the Supreme Court in Kyiv later rejected a challenge to a lower-court ruling recognising same-sex couples as de facto family. The 22 January 2026 draft Civil Code would cut across that recognition for trans people specifically, annulling a marriage on legal sex reassignment.
tangentialFactors:
Public opinion has shifted on paper. A January 2023 NDI/KIIS poll found 56% of Ukrainians supported civil partnership registration for same-sex couples; a June 2024 KIIS poll found 28.7% supported civil partnerships without adoption, 35.7% opposed and 25.6% indifferent. Broader acceptance polling among Ukrainians rose from 28% in a 2010 European study agreeing that LGBT individuals should live freely however they like to 70.4% in 2024 agreeing LGBTQ people should have the same rights, against 67.3% in 2023 and 63.7% in 2022. These figures measure attitudes among the population at large, not trans people's own reported experience.

Hostility remains organised and is documented in detail. Amnesty International's 16 May 2013 report described lawmakers being urged to vote down proposals to criminalise LGBT conduct, and attacks used as a pretext to deny rights of expression. The ex-gay movement in Ukraine holds that transgender identities as well as LGB orientations can be cured through therapeutic or religious programmes, with its largest group describing LGBTQ people as sexual perverts needing cure. Most Ukrainians affiliated with the Orthodox or Catholic Church tend to view homosexuality and non-traditional gender roles as signs of immorality, a stance compounded by the absence of fact-based sexuality education and by Soviet-era labelling of non-heterosexual relations as abnormal. The Ukrainian Council of Churches opposed the Istanbul Convention partly on grounds it could distort younger generations' sexual identity.

Pride events have required heavy state protection. Kyiv's march on 12 June 2016 drew 1,500 participants guarded by 5,500 police and 1,200 National Guard, and earlier events were cancelled in May 2012 and July 2014 over safety guarantees. Human Rights Watch noted in 2011 frequent reports of harassment and violence against LGBTQ people, with many reporting that they needed to lie about sexual orientation or gender identity to avoid discrimination, and a perception that such violence was frequently tolerated by the government; Ukrainian police hardly ever detain attackers.

Partner recognition has advanced through courts and executive statements rather than statute. A 2015 government action plan promised a civil partnership bill by 2017, but the Ministry of Justice declared in 2018 it could not proceed under pressure from religious organisations. A civil unions bill was introduced in Parliament in March 2023. After a July 2022 petition exceeding 28,000 signatures, President Zelenskyy asked the Prime Minister to review same-sex civil partnerships while stating that marriage could not be introduced during wartime because the Constitution cannot be changed under martial law; on 14 November 2024, asked by a student representative whether he would sign registered partnerships legislation, he answered "Yes!". The EU accession roadmap approved on 14 May 2025 set a Q3 2025 deadline for a registered partnerships law.

International attention to trans Ukrainians during the invasion is documented from mid-2022 onward: European Parliament written question E-002018/2022 of June 2022 raised the situation of transgender people in Ukraine amid the Russian invasion, and France 24 reported in June 2022 on Ukraine's trans community caught in the crosshairs of war. Human Rights Watch returned to the subject on 15 May 2024 with case work on war-displaced trans women.
localsOnly:
Family formation is restricted for residents. Clause 211 of the Family Code of Ukraine explicitly bans same-sex couples from adopting children, while single Ukrainian citizens of any sexual orientation are permitted to adopt; foreign adopters must be married in a registered different-sex marriage. Lesbian couples have greater parenting access than gay male couples because IVF and assisted insemination treatments are legal.

Workplace and media protections bind residents directly: the Labor Code amendment of 12 November 2015 prohibits gender identity discrimination at work, and the media bill passed unanimously in December 2022 bans hate speech and discrimination on gender identity grounds. Hate-crime aggravation in the Criminal Code still excludes gender identity, and the roadmap of 14 May 2025 only plans to add it by Q2 2026.

Document amendment for residents runs through the psychiatric system. The 2011 Civil Code amendment allowed transgender people who had undergone gender-affirming surgery to change their name to reflect gender identity, with seven surgeries and five new documents reported in 2014; since December 2016 documents issue before surgery, but a diagnosis of transsexuality, which remains classified as a psychiatric disorder, is still the entry condition, and surgery itself is legal only over 25. ZMINA's 28 July 2026 reporting indicates that obtaining that diagnosis has become harder for trans women because of stereotypes, corruption and wartime barriers.

Military obligations bear on residents with male gender markers. Homosexuality is not a legal ground for exemption from military service, and as of the Trans Forum in Kyiv in early June 2026 it remained unresolved whether being trans grounds an exemption from mobilisation. Gender Stream records that since martial law holders of male gender markers have been stopped at the border by the State Border Guard Service, and it assists residents with processing or reissue of documents for legal border crossing, alongside evacuating LGBTQI+ people and families from frontline regions to western Ukraine and the EU.

Resident organising has a long record: Ukraine's first LGBTQ rights group, Our World (Nash Svit), was created in 1998 as a community centre and human rights advocacy organisation, the Union of Gay Organizations of Ukraine coalition formed in 2008, and the Gay Alliance of Ukraine was founded in 2009. The sources describe no trans-specific facilities or shelters.
outOfScopeNotes:
The date of the Supreme Court ruling rejecting a challenge to recognition of same-sex couples as de facto family is given inconsistently across the sources, as 22 January 2026 in one and March 2026 in another. This is unresolved.

No source in this inventory addresses entry or visa rules for trans visitors, airport or border screening treatment of binders, packers, breast forms or gender presentation, or document-marker flagging at ports of entry. Nothing is claimed either way on those points.

No trans-specific violence figure with a denominator is available here, so no rate is stated. The only documented attacks in this inventory are dated June 2012, and the most recent documented instance is from 2012; no later instance is documented.

Whether the deadlines in the 14 May 2025 rule-of-law roadmap were met, specifically registered-partnership status by Q3 2025 and administrative liability plus hate-crime aggravation by Q2 2026, is not sourced.

The effect of the 22 January 2026 draft Civil Code on the transition procedure, and whether being trans exempts a person from mobilisation, were both still open questions at the Trans Forum in Kyiv in early June 2026. The draft's passage into law is not sourced.

No trans-specific shelters, facilities or dedicated care services are documented in this inventory.
